target.title: Towards reconstructing intelligible speech from the human auditory cortex

read.pdf: Published article PDF inspected: Figs. 1–5 and references; supplementary PDF inspected: Tables 1–6 and Figs. S1–S4; no tables appear in the main article PDF.

target.first_public_note: bioRxiv 10.1101/350124 v1 posted 2018-06-19 (bioRxiv API), titled "Reconstructing intelligible speech from the human auditory cortex"; journal version Scientific Reports 9:874, 2019-01.

entries.text: The authors present direct estimation of speech-synthesizer parameters from neural data as a previously unattempted reconstruction target.
entries.condition: Auditory-cortex neural responses are mapped to vocoder parameters and then synthesized as speech.
entries.quote: A natural choice is to directly estimate the parameters of a speech synthesizer from neural data, but this has not been attempted previously

entries.text: Five neurosurgical patients with epilepsy contributed ECoG data while listening to continuous speech.
entries.condition: Patients were undergoing epilepsy treatment; all self-reported normal hearing. Models were trained separately for each patient.

entries.text: Two of the five patients had high-density subdural grids, primarily over the left superior temporal gyrus.
entries.condition: Grid coverage was primarily over left STG.

entries.text: Four of the five patients had depth electrodes covering Heschl’s gyrus.
entries.condition: ECoG recordings from patients with epilepsy.

entries.text: Training stories lasted 30 minutes and were spoken by four speakers, two female.
entries.condition: In-house continuous stories used for neural-model training; story speakers were distinct from TI-46 digit speakers.

entries.text: The objective reconstruction test used eight continuous-speech sentences totaling 40 seconds.
entries.condition: Continuous speech; objective quality/intelligibility assessed with ESTOI per patient.

entries.text: Results state that objective-test sentences were repeated six times in random order and neural responses were averaged across repetitions.
entries.condition: Repeated-sentence objective test; averaging was intended to reduce neural noise.
entries.quote: The sentences were repeated six times in random order, and the neural data was averaged over the six repetitions

entries.text: Methods instead state that the eight objective-test sentences were presented eight times, conflicting with the Results repetition count.
entries.condition: Methods section, objective sentence test; Results report six repetitions for the same test.
entries.quote: Eight of the sentences (40 seconds) were used for objective tests and were presented to the patients eight times

entries.text: The TI-46 subjective test comprised 40 unique tokens: ten digits spoken by four speakers, two male and two female.
entries.unit: tokens; digit classes; speakers; speakers by gender
entries.condition: One token per digit and speaker; four model outputs were assessed; test speakers differed from story-training speakers.

entries.text: No digit sound was used to train the neural models, and TI-46 digit speakers were disjoint from the in-house story speakers.
entries.condition: The digit-recognition test is speaker-disjoint from the story-training audio, but the neural ECoG subjects are not held out: models were fitted per subject.

entries.text: Each digit stimulus was repeated six times during neural recording to improve response SNR.
entries.condition: TI-46 neural elicitation; separate from the listener test, in which each reconstructed token was heard once.
entries.quote: Each digit was repeated six times to improve the signal to noise ratio of the neural responses.

entries.text: Neural input used low-frequency 0–50 Hz and high-gamma 70–150 Hz features; the reconstruction target was sampled at 100 Hz.
entries.unit: Hz; Hz; target samples per second (Hz)
entries.condition: High-gamma envelope combined with low-frequency signal in the best-performing DNN-vocoder model.
entries.loc: Results, Reconstruction accuracy from low and high neural frequencies

entries.text: High-gamma was formed by averaging Hilbert envelopes from eight IIR-filtered bands between 70 and 150 Hz.
entries.condition: High-gamma range 70–150 Hz; envelope resampled to 100 Hz.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and neural recording

entries.text: High-gamma responses were normalized relative to a two-minute silence interval before each recording.
entries.condition: The paper does not specify corresponding normalization for low-frequency features or acoustic targets; see t46.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and neural recording

entries.text: Intracranial EEG was acquired at 3 kHz per channel with 16-bit precision and a ±8 mV range.
entries.condition: Continuous iEEG acquisition; reference was subdural or skull electrode according to bedside signal quality.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and neural recording

entries.text: Regression input was a 300 ms sliding neural window with a 10 ms hop, selected to maximize reconstruction accuracy.
entries.condition: Applied to linear and DNN regression; maximum time lag was separately set to 30 ms.

entries.text: The 516-parameter WORLD representation was compressed to a 256-dimensional autoencoder bottleneck for neural reconstruction.
entries.condition: Vocoder features included spectral envelope, pitch, voicing, and aperiodicity; reconstructed bottleneck outputs were decoded to vocoder parameters.
entries.quote: An autoencoder with a bottleneck layer was used to reduce the 516 vocoder parameters to 256.

entries.text: The vocoder autoencoder was trained separately on 80 hours of Wall Street Journal speech.
entries.condition: Separate corpus from the patient story-training and TI-46 testing data.
entries.quote: The autoencoder was trained on 80 hours of speech using a separate speech corpus (Wall Street Journal l).

entries.text: The authors report that decoding compressed autoencoder features outperformed decoding raw vocoder parameters directly.
entries.condition: Architecture ablation; values in Supplementary Table 2 (t56), read from the supplementary PDF.

entries.text: Adding Gaussian noise at the bottleneck instead of dropout/regularization performed significantly better (paired t-test, p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Autoencoder bottleneck robustness comparison; exact test sample and independent unit are not specified.

entries.text: Main networks used dropout p = 0.3 between layers.
entries.condition: Batch normalization and nonlinearities were also used; L2 multiplier is 0.001 (t54). AEC bottleneck noise was reported to outperform dropout/regularization.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, DNN training and cross validation

entries.text: Training used batches of 256 and Adam with initial learning rate 0.0001.
entries.condition: Applied to DNN training; the learning-rate schedule halves the rate after four validation-loss stalls (t55); the validation partition is not described.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, DNN training and cross validation

entries.text: Networks were trained for 150 epochs separately for each patient.
entries.condition: Per-patient LR and DNN models; no number of repeated random initializations is given.
entries.quote: Network training was achieved in 150 epochs and was performed for each subject separately.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, DNN training and cross validation

entries.text: The maximum time lag used was 30 ms; the loss combined MSE and Pearson correlation.
entries.condition: DNN regression; loss was defined per sample over acoustic labels.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, DNN training and cross validation

entries.text: The authors say LR and DNN used cross-validation, with stories for training and repeated sentences plus digit sounds for testing.
entries.condition: Digit sounds excluded from training; digit speakers differed from story speakers; fold count and exact partitioning are not given (t43).

entries.text: Eleven normal-hearing listeners evaluated 160 reconstructed digit tokens in randomized order across four models.
entries.condition: Tokens comprised ten digits from four speakers; each listener heard each digit once, reported digit/uncertain, MOS quality, and speaker gender.
entries.quote: We asked 11 subjects with normal hearing to listen to the reconstructed digits from all four models (160 tokens total) in a random order.

entries.text: Listeners reported digit identity or uncertainty, rated MOS on a 1–5 scale, and identified speaker gender; each reconstructed token was heard once.
entries.condition: Human listening, headphones, quiet environment; no ASR decoder, language model, or lexical rescoring is described.
entries.loc: Results, Subjective evaluation; Materials and Methods, Subjective and objective evaluations

entries.text: DNN-vocoder achieved 75% digit accuracy and was reported as 67% higher than the linear-regression/auditory-spectrogram baseline.
entries.unit: % correct digit reports; % relative improvement over baseline as stated
entries.condition: Closed-set zero-to-nine listening test; 40 unique TI-46 tokens, four speakers disjoint from story training, 11 normal-hearing listeners, each token heard once; DNN-vocoder used low- plus high-frequency neural features; no LM.
entries.quote: The DNN-vocoder combination achieved the best performance (75% accuracy), which is 67% higher than the baseline system (Linear regression with auditory spectrogram).

entries.text: The abstract instead reports a 65% intelligibility improvement over the same linear-regression/auditory-spectrogram baseline.
entries.condition: Abstract’s closed-set digit-recognition comparison; Results report 67% (t28).
entries.quote: improving the intelligibility by 65% over the baseline method which used linear regression to reconstruct the auditory spectrogram.

entries.text: Across the two representations, DNN models averaged 68.5% digit accuracy versus 47.5% for LR (paired t-test, p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Subjective closed-set digit test; four model conditions, 40 unique tokens, 11 listeners; aggregation and statistical unit are not specified.

entries.text: DNN-vocoder MOS was 3.4 versus 2.5, 2.3, and 2.1 for the other systems (unpaired t-test, p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Eleven normal-hearing listeners rated the same randomized 160-token closed-set digit test; other values correspond to the other three model combinations.

entries.text: DNN-vocoder speaker-gender identification was 80% and above chance (t-test, p < 0.001); other models were described as at chance.
entries.condition: Four TI-46 test speakers, two male and two female; 11 listeners; numeric chance level is not reported (t47).

entries.text: For objective ESTOI on continuous-speech test sentences, DNN models outperformed LR and vocoder reconstruction outperformed auditory-spectrogram reconstruction (t-test, p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Eight 40-second sentences; per-patient ECoG models; neural responses averaged across repeated presentations, with Results/METHODS repeat-count discrepancy t7–t8.
entries.loc: Results, Objective evaluation of reconstructed audio

entries.text: The authors report that the relative ESTOI ranking of the four models was consistent across all five patients, despite inter-patient accuracy variation.
entries.condition: Objective continuous-speech evaluation; authors attribute inter-patient variation as likely related to auditory-cortical coverage.
entries.quote: This pattern was consistent for each of the five subjects in this study, as shown in Fig. 4B alongside the electrode locations for each subject.

entries.text: Reported neural-network improvements over linear models for individual vocoder parameters were pitch 157.2%, aperiodicity 18.5%, spectral envelope 6.2%, and voiced-unvoiced 0.15%.
entries.unit: % improvement over linear model (parameter-specific; metric basis not specified)
entries.condition: Supplementary Fig. 3 labels reconstruction accuracy as Pearson correlation; the text's percentage-improvement calculation and aggregation are not specified.

entries.text: Combining low-frequency and high-gamma features significantly outperformed either band alone on ESTOI (p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Only DNN-auditory-spectrogram model; objective continuous-speech test; band conditions were high-gamma, low-frequency, and both.
entries.quote: We found that the combination of the two frequency bands significantly outperforms the reconstruction from only one of the frequency bands (Fig. 5A, p < 0.001, t-test).
entries.loc: Results, Reconstruction accuracy from low and high neural frequencies

entries.text: Electrode-count experiment pooled electrodes across all five patients and tested N = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, with 20 random subsets per N; accuracy rose with diminishing gains.
entries.condition: Pooled across patients; individual networks trained on each subset; averaged ESTOI used for comparison.
entries.quote: randomly chose N electrodes (N = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128), twenty times for training the individual networks.
entries.loc: Results, Effect of the number of electrodes and duration of training data

entries.text: Training-duration experiment used 128 random electrodes, segments reported as 10–30 minutes, and 20 random subsets per duration; Fig. 5C also shows a 5-minute tick.
entries.unit: electrodes; minutes; random subsets per condition
entries.condition: ESTOI averaged across random training-data segments; test set remained continuous speech.
entries.loc: Results, Effect of the number of electrodes and duration of training data; Fig. 5C

entries.text: The authors report that reconstruction accuracy increased as the duration of training data increased.
entries.condition: Training-duration analysis used 128 electrodes and 20 randomly selected segments per duration (t38).
entries.loc: Results, Effect of the number of electrodes and duration of training data

entries.text: Authors concede that training duration was limited and more data might be needed before added electrodes provide further benefit.
entries.condition: A limitation on interpreting the electrode-count scaling experiment.

entries.text: The demonstrated intelligibility is closed-set; continuous, open-set natural speech requires further research.
entries.condition: The main human evaluation was recognition of the ten TI-46 digits, not open-vocabulary speech communication.

entries.text: The authors state that systems need further design and training work to generalize between overt and covert conditions; this study evaluated listening to speech, not imagined speech.
entries.condition: No covert-speech evaluation was reported in this study.

entries.text: The authors describe the combination of broad brain coverage, more training data, and both neural bands as an upper-bound setting constrained by practical access limitations.
entries.condition: They note limited brain coverage and lack of accessible high-frequency signals in noninvasive neuroimaging as practical constraints.

entries.text: The paper does not report cross-validation fold count, exact train/validation/test partition assignments, or how repeated sentences were kept independent across folds.
entries.condition: Cross-validation is named, and stories versus repeated sentences/digits are broadly separated, but detailed fold protocol is absent.

entries.text: Random seeds are not reported for primary model initialization, the 20 random subset draws, or listener trial order; the number of independently retrained LR/DNN models is also unstated.

questions.q: Which repetition count was actually used for the eight-sentence objective test: six or eight presentations?
questions.answer: Results state six repetitions and Methods state eight. Supplementary Fig. S1 plots averages through six repetitions, but the article does not explicitly reconcile the count of presentations.

questions.q: Why does the abstract report a 65% intelligibility improvement while the Results report 67%?
questions.answer: Both values are stated against the same linear-regression/auditory-spectrogram baseline; the paper does not explain the difference or provide a calculation that reconciles them.

questions.q: Was the subjective reconstruction test based on one patient, a selected patient, or an aggregation of outputs across patients?
questions.answer: Not stated; the networks are said to be trained per patient, while the listening protocol presents 40 tokens per model without identifying the source patient or aggregation.

questions.q: How many listeners contributed to the subjective experiment, and why does the consistency statement say ten when the study otherwise reports eleven?
questions.answer: The experiment is described as n=11 in the methods and figure caption, but the Results consistency statement says ten; no explanation is given.

questions.q: What were the cross-validation folds, model-selection partitions, and random seeds for the reported model comparisons?
questions.answer: The paper names cross-validation and a validation-loss schedule, but does not report fold assignments, the validation/selection dataset, or primary-run seeds and repeats.

questions.q: What numeric chance levels and scoring rule were used for uncertain digit responses?
questions.answer: The paper gives ten digit labels plus an uncertain response and says gender results exceed chance, but does not give numeric chance baselines or explain how uncertain responses enter the digit-accuracy denominator.
